steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a chapter that critically examines the common ML narrative that artificial neural networks learn and represent human concepts. It should lay out the narrative, explain why I was skeptical, and preview the chapter's conclusions on its key assumptions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- The narrative in the ML community about what ANNs represent
- Evidence people have found for it
- Why it would matter if true
- My skepticism
- Structure of the chapter: three assumptions and conclusions
- Aims and what is out of scope

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- The narrative (shared by large parts of ML community) about representational qualities of ANNs
  - 1. ANNs do tasks only humans could do before: classifying videos, producing human-like text
  - 2. humans rely on concepts = higher order representations for these tasks; images as composed of objects; texts as following abstract grammatical rules
  - 3. to do the same tasks, ANNs must have developed the same concepts
  - 4. concepts represented in weights, units, filters, channels, or layers -- depends on architecture and who you ask
- Evidence people searched for
  - early CNN layers reassemble / exactly match human-engineered edge detectors
  - later CNN units co-activate with complex concepts in images (wheels, grass)
  - text classifiers: neurons connected to sentiment
  - LLMs: factual knowledge largely in mid-layer modules; neurons connected to space and time
- Significance if true
  - practical + philosophical
  - explains why ANNs work so well: they develop the right concepts
  - human concepts incl. natural kinds arise naturally from efficiently solving complex prediction tasks
  - how empiricist philosophy can explain human cognition
- Skepticism (questions)
  - aren't neural nets just estimators of conditional densities?
  - are our concepts so natural that ANNs must learn exactly the same ones?
  - wasn't the point of ANNs to distribute meaning, not store it in individual units?
- Literature search / chapter structure
  - ML researchers vague about what representation of learned human concepts means -> no testable hypotheses, anecdotal evidence
  - chapter structured along three key assumptions; conclusions given up front
  - I: ANNs work well -- theory shaky, but strong empirical evidence they are solid approximations of best possible predictors in static data settings (Section 3)
  - II: ANNs learn human concepts -- evidence for (transfer learning) and against (adversarial examples); likely learn both human and non-human concepts (Section 4)
  - III: represented by single units -- evidence very weak; units only weakly coactivate with concepts, don't share functional role (Section 5)
- Aims / scope
  - first: clarity on representational qualities of current ANNs based on evidence
  - second: conceptual guidance for ML researchers on notion of representation of learned human concepts -> falsifiable hypotheses, more evidence for I-III
  - not covered: whether ANNs similar to biological neural nets; how humans store/process concepts; pointers for interested readers

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
A lot of people in the machine learning (ML) community seem to share a narrative about what Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) represent. It goes roughly like this:

1. ANNs can do tasks that in the past only humans could do, for example classifying videos or producing text that looks human-like.

2. When humans do these tasks, they use concepts, meaning higher order representations. Humans see images as made of objects. They think of texts as following abstract grammatical rules.

3. So to do the same tasks as humans, ANNs must have developed the same concepts that humans have.

4. These concepts are represented in the weights, units, filters, channels, or layers of the ANNs. Which one it is depends on the model architecture and also on who you ask.

People then started looking for evidence for this narrative. They found that the early layers of trained Convolutional Neural Nets (CNNs) closely reassemble the edge detectors that human engineers designed, or even match them exactly. Units later in CNNs co-activate with some complex concepts in images, like wheels or grass. Text classifiers have neurons connected to the sentiment of the text, and Large Language Models (LLMs) seem to store factual knowledge mostly in mid-layer modules and also have neurons connected to space and time.

If this narrative is correct, it would be very significant both practically and philosophically. It would explain why ANNs work so well, because they just develop the right concepts. It would show that human concepts, our natural kinds included, really do come up naturally when you solve complex prediction tasks efficiently. And it would explain how empiricist philosophy can explain human cognition.

- My skepticism: neural nets just estimators of conditional densities? concepts so natural that ANNs must learn exactly the same? point of ANNs was to distribute meaning, not store in individual units?
- went through ML literature on concept representation in ANNs
  - researchers vague on what representation of learned human concepts means -> no testable hypotheses, anecdotal evidence
  - chapter structured by three key assumptions behind narrative; conclusions up front
  - I, ANNs work well: theory shaky; strong empirical evidence they are solid approximations of best possible predictors in static data settings (Section 3)
  - II, ANNs learn human concepts: for (transfer learning), against (adversarial examples); likely both human and non-human concepts (Section 4)
  - III, single units represent them: evidence very weak; units weakly coactivate, don't share functional role (Section 5)
- aims: clarity based on evidence; conceptual guidance -> falsifiable hypotheses, further evidence for I-III
- out of scope: similarity to biological neural nets, how humans store/process concepts -> pointers

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
A lot of people in the machine learning (ML) community seem to share a narrative about what Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) represent. It goes roughly like this:

1. ANNs can do tasks that in the past only humans could do, for example classifying videos or producing text that looks human-like.

2. When humans do these tasks, they use concepts, meaning higher order representations. Humans see images as made of objects. They think of texts as following abstract grammatical rules.

3. So to do the same tasks as humans, ANNs must have developed the same concepts that humans have.

4. These concepts are represented in the weights, units, filters, channels, or layers of the ANNs. Which one it is depends on the model architecture and also on who you ask.

People then started looking for evidence for this narrative. They found that the early layers of trained Convolutional Neural Nets (CNNs) closely reassemble the edge detectors that human engineers designed, or even match them exactly. Units later in CNNs co-activate with some complex concepts in images, like wheels or grass. Text classifiers have neurons connected to the sentiment of the text, and Large Language Models (LLMs) seem to store factual knowledge mostly in mid-layer modules and also have neurons connected to space and time.

If this narrative is correct, it would be very significant both practically and philosophically. It would explain why ANNs work so well, because they just develop the right concepts. It would show that human concepts, our natural kinds included, really do come up naturally when you solve complex prediction tasks efficiently. And it would explain how empiricist philosophy can explain human cognition.

But I was skeptical. Aren't neural nets really just estimators of conditional densities? Are our concepts actually so natural that ANNs need to learn exactly the same ones? And wasn't the whole point of using ANNs that meaning is distributed, rather than stored in individual units?

So I started to look through the ML literature on how concepts are represented in ANNs. What I found is that ML researchers stay vague about what they mean when they talk about representing learned human concepts, so they don't give testable hypotheses, just anecdotal evidence. I structured my search, and so also this chapter, along three key assumptions that I found underneath the narrative above. Here are my conclusions about them already:

- Assumption I, ANNs work well: The theoretical grounds are still shaky, but there is strong empirical evidence that ANNs are solid approximations of the best possible predictors in static data settings (See Section 3).

- Assumption II, ANNs learn human concepts: There is evidence for this claim (e.g. transfer learning) and there is also evidence against it (e.g. adversarial examples). Probably ANNs learn some human concepts and some non-human concepts (See Section 4).

- Assumption III, ANNs represent these learned human concepts by single units: Some evidence could be read as supporting the claim, but it turns out to be very weak. Individual units that should represent concepts often coactivate only weakly with them and don't have the same functional role (See Section 5).

The goal is first to give clarity, based on evidence, about the representational qualities of current ANNs. The second goal is to give ML researchers some conceptual guidance on the notion of representing learned human concepts, hoping this helps them form falsifiable hypotheses and collect more evidence for assumptions I-III.

I will not discuss whether ANNs are in any way similar to biological neural nets, and I will also not discuss how humans store or process concepts. Readers who are interested in these questions can look at other work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large parts of the machine learning (ML) community seem to share a remarkable narrative about the representational qualities of Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) [1,2]:

- 1. ANNs can perform tasks that only humans could perform in the past, such as classifying videos or producing human-like text.

- 2. When humans perform these tasks, they rely on concepts, meaning higher order representations. Humans perceive images as composed of objects. They think of texts as following abstract grammatical rules.

- 3. To do the same tasks as humans, ANNs must have developed the same concepts as humans.

- 4. These concepts are represented in the weights, units, filters, channels, or layers of the ANNs, depending on the model architecture and on who you ask.

And indeed, people started searching for evidence in favor of this narrative. They found that early layers in trained Convolutional Neural Nets (CNNs) closely reassemble or even exactly match edge detectors designed by human engineers [3]. Later units in CNNs co-activate with some complex concepts found in images, such as wheels or grass [4]. Text classifiers have neurons that are connected to the sentiment in texts [5], and Large Language Models (LLMs) seem to store factual knowledge largely in mid-layer modules [6] and have neurons connected to space and time [7].

If the narrative were correct, it would have great practical and philosophical significance: It would explain why ANNs work so well – they simply develop the right concepts [2]; It would show that human concepts, including our natural kinds [8], really arise naturally from efficiently solving complex prediction tasks [9]; Moreover, it would show how empiricist philosophy can explain human cognition [10].

Yet, I remained skeptical: Aren't neural nets just estimators of conditional densities? Are our concepts really so natural that ANNs have to learn exactly the same concepts? Wasn't the point of using ANNs to distribute meaning rather than store it in individual units?

I therefore started to examine the ML literature on concept representation in ANNs. I found that ML researchers remain vague about what they mean by the representation of learned human concepts, and so they do not provide testable hypotheses, but rather anecdotal evidence [11]. I have structured my search, and consequently this chapter, along the three key assumptions I found underlying the narrative above. I already give my conclusions about these assumptions here:

- • Assumption I, ANNs work well: Even though the theoretical grounds are still shaky, there is strong empirical evidence that ANNs are solid approximations of the best possible predictors in static data settings (See Section 3).

- • Assumption II, ANNs learn human concepts: There is evidence in favor of this claim (e.g. transfer learning) as well as evidence against it (e.g. adversarial examples). It is likely that ANNs learn some human and some non-human concepts (See Section 4).

- • Assumption III, ANNs represent these learned human concepts by single units: Some evidence could be interpreted in favor of the claim, but it turns out to be very weak. Individual units that are supposed to represent concepts often only weakly coactivate with them and do not share their functional role (See Section 5).

The aim is, first, to provide clarity on the representational qualities of current ANNs based on evidence, and second, to give ML researchers conceptual guidance on the notion of the representation of learned human concepts, in the hope of helping them form falsifiable hypotheses and gather further evidence for assumptions I-III.

In this work, I will not touch on the question whether ANNs are in any way similar to biological neural nets, and I will not discuss how humans store or process concepts. Readers interested in these questions are pointed to [12,10,13] or [14].
